title: Architecture and TRD criteria
introduction: One list. The solutions architect develops the architecture, its detailed design and the TRD to it, and reviews and approves them against it; the spec authors develop the specs to it, and the spec review reviews them against it. Nothing is reviewed against anything else. Each criterion has a level and a home document, and is satisfied by its home document.

levels.heading: Architecture and design: arc42 and the detailed architecture
The specs and the Tasks
levels.note: These are not part of the architecture. A spec and a Task carry what their work builds from the architecture and design documents, by link or as stated there; they decide no design.

criteria.text: The acceptance basis is the PRD's business outcomes, settled owner decisions, the section 2 constraints and the documentation model's obligations.
A mechanism named in a PRD is a design input, not a business requirement.

The solutions architect decides technical gaps with cited evidence, asking a specialist when the gap needs one. Only business requirements that no design can meet together, or a conflict with section 2, reach the owner.
AWS behaviour is established from AWS documentation through the AWS MCP Server. State assumptions, tradeoffs and regional applicability. Never invent scale.

Cite an arc42 statement by path and heading, guidance by URL, and code by repository, revision and file:line. Code that no pipeline built is a hint and is never evidence that arc42 is wrong; only code the matrix marks built or deployed is expected to match.
One design fact lives in one home. Every other document links to it.
Never write section 2. Only architecture-maintainer writes arc42 and the detailed architecture. A script promotes.

A finding names the criterion id, the item, the observation with its path and heading, and a bounded correction with a condition that shows it is done. A preference is not a finding. Something no criterion requires is not a finding.

A review covers only content that is not yet approved. Approved content is reference: it is reported only when an unapproved item cannot be correct unless an approved statement is wrong. A re-check covers only the corrected items.

No architecture decision is made by instinct. Every AWS resource the design defines is reviewed with the AWS tools (the AWS MCP servers and the aws-core skills) against AWS best practice and security best practice, the design has a Well-Architected review, and every decision between two or more options states the options considered and the reason for the choice; each is recorded in the Epic's review log, to the log-architecture-review skill's schema.

Anyone who specifies or builds the work can name, from the architecture and design documents, the building block, its repository and stack, the owner of each store, each interface and its caller, and each event type and its publisher without inventing a design.
Section 5 names each building block the PRD needs, what it is responsible for and what it owns. Each store has one owning block and a statement of what it holds.
Each interface is named with the block that exposes it and who may call it. Trust boundaries are explicit: who may call each boundary and what each runtime may call.
Each event type is named in the event catalog with its producers and description, and each routing rule names the event types it matches (or all), its targets and the stack that owns it.

Section 6 shows, for each important scenario and each failure the PRD's outcomes depend on, which building blocks interact and in what order. Retry, dead-letter and idempotent behaviour are stated as behaviour.
Section 7 says where each block runs and which stack holds each resource. Values shared between stacks are named as shared, by the mechanism section 2 fixes.
Each rule that applies across blocks is a design fact in section 8 with its reason, in the form "Because of X, the address is verified by Y".
No fact is stated in two documents. Section 6 links to a rule; it does not restate it.

Every behaviour a shared service, component, layer or library provides is taken from it, by the shared-home rule of arc42 section 4 (04-solution-strategy). Each shared home's section 5 document states under "Provides" what consumers obtain from it and must not implement.

The front matter of each document records the catalog keys the documentation model states for its document class: a view records view_type, scope, subject, shows and lifecycle_state; a standard or policy records document_class: standard or document_class: policy and lifecycle_state, and has no view_type, scope or shows.
Names of blocks, stores, interfaces and event types agree across documents.

Each document holds the facts of its one subject, in the place the architecture documentation model gives them: in arc42 when the statement stays true if the code is rewritten, otherwise in its document under detailed/ (one component, one feature, components working together, or the whole system), linked from the arc42 view of its subject.
The design meets each PRD outcome it concerns and no section 2 constraint is broken.
Each diagram renders, is readable, and agrees with the text beside it.
Where the design has an interface, each route has its method, path, authorizer, request and response fields and status codes in the detailed design of the component that exposes it.

Where the design has a store, it has its key attribute names, indexes, access patterns and expiry attribute, and its logical or physical data model, in the detailed design of the component that owns it.
Where the design publishes an event, its publishing service and the values passed to the project's event-publishing API are in the detailed design of the publishing component.

Configuration names, SSM parameter names, and log, metric and alarm names the design introduces are in the detailed design of the component that uses them, each generated with the project's naming command.
Idempotency key fields and timeout settings are in the detailed design of the component that applies them; a timeout is the value its TRD requirement states.

Where the work needs it, a component's internal structure (its classes or modules, object and data models with their attributes and types, and the lifecycle of its entities) is drawn in its detailed design, in the view types the documentation model's list names for it.
Every requirement has a stable id, a kind, a statement with a checkable value, a source and the element it applies to.

Where the design has the element, the TRD carries its obligations: availability, latency, security controls, retention, recovery, limits, timeouts and retry counts, that logs, metrics and alarms exist, and cost constraints. Cost unit math is kept as evidence in the solutions architect's result.
Each shared capability the design uses has one requirement of kind `reuse` naming the element, the behaviour and the capability.
No requirement contradicts an effective arc42 statement or section 2, and none creates an element.
Every PRD requirement that needs a technical obligation has one.
A requirement says what, with a value. It does not say how, and it holds no name or shape that belongs to the architecture and design documents.
Each route has its method, path, authorizer, request and response fields and status codes as the detailed design records them.
Each store has its key attribute names, indexes, access patterns and expiry attribute as the detailed design records them.
Each event names its publishing service and has the values passed to the project's event-publishing API as the detailed design records them.
Configuration names, SSM parameter names, and log, metric and alarm names are present as the detailed design records them.
Idempotency key fields and timeout settings are stated as the detailed design records them.

Each contract this repository shares with another repository (a route it exposes or calls, an event it publishes or a routing rule matches) names the other repository's element, and its fields are exactly those of the other repository's spec where that spec exists. An event contract names no consumer: a producer's spec names no routing rule or target, and a routing rule's spec names the event types it matches.
A Task can name the repository, stack, handler, table, route, event and the shared capabilities it must use without inventing a design.
